items.title: Asia in Focus China H2 Fiscal Outlook Reversing the Tightening

**Negative Fiscal Impulse in Q2**: Fiscal impulse turned negative due to slowed government bond issuance/spending, contributing nearly half the GDP slowdown (Q2 growth 3.6% qoq vs Q1 5.0% yoy), offsetting export strength.

**Local Implementation Risks**: Local officials’ risk aversion (record-high anti-corruption proxies, post-disaster caution from Lushenyu coal disaster, Shanxi explosion) and implementation constraints undermine fiscal stimulus effectiveness.

**Growth Target Achievable with Conditional Stimulus**: 4.5-5.0% full-year target remains on track (H1 GDP 4.7% yoy), prioritizing *pace* of planned easing over new stimulus; broad measures unlikely unless growth weakens further.
**Supply-Side Policy Focus**: Spending tilted toward tech, green transition, and "Two Majors" investment (boosting 2026 GDP +50bp+), with consumption support secondary despite recent rhetoric.

items.title: Global Markets Daily What Could Spark a Reset Higher in FX Vol
summary_points: **FX Volatility Reset Triggers**: Resets occur only when growth expectations deteriorate across equities, commodities, and rates, driven by liquidity crises (30% equity sell-offs) or supply shocks; demand/policy shocks cause broad cross-asset volatility spikes.

**Current FX Volatility Anomaly**: FX volatility (EUR/USD, GBP/USD, USD/JPY) at 20-year lows despite AI, energy, and Fed uncertainty, contrasting with historical correlation where volatility spikes coincided with equity/commodity/interest rate stress.

**Divergence from Historical Patterns**: Recent cross-asset volatility spikes (equities, commodities) have not triggered sharp FX volatility resets, indicating a structural or temporary deviation in market dynamics versus past episodes (e.g., 2008 GFC, 2020 Covid).

**Growth Expectations as Key Constraint**: Stable growth sentiment across US, China, and Euro area has suppressed FX volatility, unlike historical periods where weaker growth pricing drove spikes—highlighting growth sentiment as a critical volatility determinant.

items.title: Global Economics Comment More Chinese Exports, Fewer Chinese Imports, Lower Global Inflation

**Trade-Price Channel Quantified**: A 1pp rise in Chinese exports as % of recipient consumption lowers goods prices by 0.5%; a 1pp drop in China’s global import share lowers prices by 1.3%, driving aggregate disinflation.
**Import Substitution Accelerates Disinflation**: China’s import decline (e.g., autos/clothing down 40-50% vs.
trend) reduces global supply, with 1% higher foreign goods supply lowering consumer prices by 0.8%—highlighting structural supply-side pressure.
**Trade Dynamics to Persist**: Effects not yet fully reflected in prices; widening current account surplus will push DM inflation toward target levels, delaying central bank easing.
